steps.title: Putting the whole unit to work
body: This unit gave you a lot of separate pieces: relative clauses, all ten sisters of إنّ, resumptive and attached pronouns. Real Arabic writing doesn't use them one at a time — it strings several together into a connected story, the same way ثُمَّ and أَخِيرًا already let you connect sentences back in A2.

The paragraph ahead uses a relative clause with a nominal predicate, كَانَ, and three different sisters of إنّ (لٰكِنَّ, أَنَّ, لَعَلَّ) — all in four sentences, all built from words you already know.
Read it as a story first, not as a grammar hunt. The comprehension questions after will check what you understood, not which particle did what.

steps.title: A teacher's trip
steps.intro: Read the whole story once for the gist, then again for detail. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: The main idea
steps.prompt: What is this paragraph mainly about?

options.label: A teacher who traveled to a distant city and visited a garden
A book about a famous garden
A teacher who stayed home because of bad weather

steps.explanation: The paragraph follows one trip start to finish: traveling to the city, the weather, hearing about the garden, and going there.

steps.title: A detail
steps.prompt: According to the paragraph, how was the weather in the evening?
steps.explanation: لٰكِنَّهُ دَافِئٌ فِي الْمَسَاءِ — "but it's warm in the evening," contrasting the cold morning.

steps.title: Sequence
steps.prompt: What did the man do right after hearing that the garden was beautiful?

options.label: He went back to the city
He wrote a book about it

steps.explanation: ثُمَّ ذَهَبَ إِلَى الْحَدِيقَةِ — "then he went to the garden," right after the sentence about hearing it was beautiful.

steps.title: b1-u2 is complete
steps.message: Relative clauses, singular and plural, subject and object; all ten sisters of إنّ; and now joining them into a connected story. Dual relative pronouns stay deferred past B1, the same way Form IX did for verb forms.
